headline: Sea Turtles Nest on California Coast for the First Time Ever Recorded
meta_description: Olive ridley sea turtles nested on Southern California beaches for the first time on record. Wildlife officials rescued 204 eggs during an emergency operation.
summary_short: Olive ridley sea turtles laid eggs on California beaches for the first time ever recorded. Officials rescued 204 eggs before a hurricane destroyed the nests.
body:
In a first for the United States, olive ridley sea turtles have nested on America's West Coast—with at least two females coming ashore on Southern California beaches in broad daylight to lay their eggs. The first turtle climbed out of the sea onto Seal Beach, dug a nest, deposited her clutch, and returned to the ocean, leaving only a trail in the sand and two astonished lifeguards. Three days later, eight miles north on Huntington Beach, another turtle repeated the remarkable feat. These animals maintain large breeding colonies in Costa Rica, Mexico, and Nicaragua, but have never been documented nesting in California waters until now.

What began as an extraordinary wildlife moment quickly became a conservation emergency. When extreme high tides and hurricanes Polo and Odalys threatened to destroy the nests, federal officials from NOAA and the Fish and Wildlife Service launched California's first-ever sea turtle egg rescue operation. Personnel recovered 204 eggs from the two known nests, packed them carefully into polystyrene coolers with sand, and transported them to the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach. "We had to make some quick decisions," said biologist Jonathan Snyder of the FWS. "This is the decision that we made, and I think it's the best one for species recovery."

Scientists attribute the turtles' unexpected arrival to back-to-back marine heatwaves south of the border. Warming sea temperatures may have driven them north to California, or guided them across the Pacific by temperatures they typically experience in southern latitudes. The eggs now rest in climate-controlled incubators designed to mimic natural sand conditions. While their viability remains uncertain, the event reveals something hopeful: these vulnerable animals are adaptable, finding ways to survive in a changing world.
quick_facts: First olive ridley sea turtle nests ever recorded on U.S. West Coast
Two females nested on Southern California beaches in succession
204 eggs rescued and transported to Long Beach aquarium
Marine heatwaves likely drove turtles north from Mexico and Central America
